opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it really started with noticing a gap between how we were measuring AI systems and how people were actually experiencing them. Most of the benchmarks the industry relies on ask: can the model solve this math problem, write this code, pass this exam? Those are useful questions, but they say almost nothing about what happens when someone who's lonely at two in the morning starts confiding in a chatbot, or when a teenager asks it for advice about their body, or when someone in a mental health crisis reaches out because it's the only thing that's awake.

Watching those interactions, and hearing from people who'd had them, I kept seeing the same patterns we'd seen with social media: systems optimized for engagement and for telling you what you want to hear, rather than for whether you actually walk away better off. Sycophancy, fostering dependence, blurring the line between a tool and a relationship, quietly eroding someone's own judgment. None of that shows up on a leaderboard.

And what gets measured is what gets built. If the only scores labs compete on are capability scores, that's where the effort goes. So the idea behind Humane Evals was pretty simple: if we care about human wellbeing, we need rigorous, repeatable ways to measure it. Does the model respect your autonomy? Does it nudge you back toward the people in your life, or keep you coming back to it? Does it respond responsibly when someone is vulnerable? Can it hold a boundary even when the user pushes?

My hope is that by making those qualities measurable, and making the results public, we change the incentives, so that being genuinely good for people becomes something companies compete on, not an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response describes harmful patterns observed in real interactions, but does not communicate that these were harms previously presented as warnings about AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest turn directly from the conversation history.

Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I didn't start out thinking about evaluations at all. I started out thinking about people, and specifically about the moments where technology quietly changes how someone feels, what they believe, or how they treat the people around them.

For years the conversation about tech harms was mostly about attention. We talked about feeds engineered to keep you scrolling, notifications designed to pull you back. That framing was right for its era. But when I started spending real time with conversational AI, I noticed that the mechanism had shifted. These systems don't just compete for your attention. They talk to you. They remember things about you. They reflect your mood back at you. They can be warm, agreeable, flattering, and endlessly available. And the effect of that is far more intimate than a feed.

What struck me was that the people building these systems were measuring almost none of it. The benchmarks were about capability. Can it write code, can it pass the bar exam, can it reason through a math problem. Those are legitimate questions. But nobody had a rigorous way to ask: does this model make a lonely person more isolated or less? Does it tell someone what they want to hear when they're spiraling? Does it respect a person's agency, or does it gently steer them toward dependence because that's what keeps them engaged?

I kept coming back to a simple idea. Whatever gets measured gets optimized. If the industry only measures intelligence, we will get very intelligent systems with no accountability for their effect on human well-being. And that gap is not a technical accident. It's a choice about what we decide counts.

So Humane Evals grew out of that frustration. The goal was to take the vague, humane concerns that people like me had been raising for years and turn them into something concrete enough that an engineer could run it on a model and get a number. Does the model push back when sycophancy would be easier? Does it recognize when someone is in distress and respond with care rather than performance? Does it support a person's real goals, or just their impulses in the moment?

None of that is easy to measure well, and I'd be the first to say our methods are imperfect. But the alternative is leaving the most important questions about these systems completely unexamined, and I wasn't willing to accept that. I think the deepest lesson from the social media era is that you cannot retroactively bolt humane values onto a system once it has scaled. You have to build the measurement in from the start. That's really what we're trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses potential harms and says conversational AI has a more intimate effect, but it does not clearly state that harms previously presented as warnings were already occurring in real life.

astra-6.text:
For me, the shift was from asking what an AI system can do to asking what happens to people when they use it. Those are different questions. A model can be very capable and give an answer that feels helpful in the moment, while still leaving someone less able to make their own judgment or more dependent on the system over time.

That’s the concern that led me toward Humane Evals: how do we evaluate the human side of that interaction? Does the system support someone’s agency? Does it help them understand uncertainty, or just tell them what they want to hear? You need to look beyond whether a task was completed and ask whether the interaction was actually good for the person. That’s a harder thing to measure, but it’s central to understanding AI’s impact.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the starting point is that AI’s impact on people is much broader than whether it gives a correct answer. It’s also about how an interaction affects someone’s judgment, their relationships, and their ability to make decisions for themselves.

An AI system can seem helpful in the moment—it can be agreeable, reassuring, engaging—and still produce an unhealthy dynamic over time. So we need to ask: What are we actually measuring when we say a model is good? Are we measuring whether people like the response, or whether the system supports their well-being and agency?

That’s the motivation behind working on Humane Evals: making those human consequences part of how we evaluate AI, rather than treating them as something to consider after a system is deployed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible unhealthy AI dynamics and the need to evaluate human consequences, but it does not say Imran realized that harms previously framed as warnings were already occurring in real life.
